hints: Resolve the launch velocity $V$ at angle $\theta$ into horizontal $V\cos\theta$ and vertical $V\sin\theta$ components for the P to Q flight.
Use vertical motion with zero net vertical displacement at Q to find the total time of flight in terms of $V\sin\theta$ and $g$.
Multiply the constant horizontal velocity by that total time to form $R$, then check that your expression has units of metres.
walkthrough: Resolve $V$: horizontal velocity $v_x = V\cos\theta$ is constant because air resistance is negligible, and initial vertical velocity $u_y = V\sin\theta$ upwards.
For the vertical motion from P to Q the displacement is zero, so use $s_y = u_y t + \frac{1}{2}at^2$ with $s_y = 0$ and $a = -g$.
Then $0 = V\sin\theta \times T - \frac{1}{2}gT^2$, so the non-zero total time is $T = 2V\sin\theta/g$.
Horizontal range is constant velocity times total time: $R = v_x T = (V\cos\theta)(2V\sin\theta/g)$.
Simplifying gives $R = 2V^2\sin\theta\cos\theta/g$. This is option B.

A.explanation: This is half the full range because it uses only the time to reach maximum height, not the total time from P to Q.

B.explanation: Horizontal speed $V\cos\theta$ multiplied by total flight time $2V\sin\theta/g$ gives $R = 2V^2\sin\theta\cos\theta/g$.

C.explanation: This is one quarter of the correct range and has an extra factor of 2 in the denominator.

D.explanation: This is dimensionally wrong because $V^2 g$ has units $\text{m}^3\text{s}^{-4}$, so $R$ would not be in metres.
